events.title: Proposed ruling: refund_full $6.61 (model confidence 0.93)
events.body:
This is a no-show cancellation-fee dispute: the driver cancelled and the rider was charged $6.61 [F4][F7]. claims.assertion: The driver cancelled the trip as a no-show, but the record shows no arrival confirmation at all: nobody tapped "I'm Here" and the platform recorded no automatic arrival (driver_pressed_here_at is null), so NS-1(i) fails and the $6.61 must be returned in full.

The driver's own written admission ('I forgot to press the I'm Here button but I was there') confirms the mandatory arrival button was never pressed, and a driver's statement cannot supply an element the system record shows is missing.

The platform arrived at most 22:41:30 and the driver cancelled at 22:46:50 (F4), so the wait on the record was 5 min 20 s — but NS-2 applies because the (i) precondition, a valid arrival confirmation, was never met; this is not a case about wait length.
The $6.61 cancellation fee was actually charged (F7), so the rider's loss is live and the refund requested is exactly the fee on the fare record, without any surge component (F8).
The dispute was filed promptly (rider has no prior upheld or pending fee-related history in the 90-day window) and the remedy under NS-7 is a $6.61 voucher rather than cash.
No incident, injury or dangerous-driving element appears anywhere in the chat or the driver's statement, so this is an ordinary fee dispute, not a SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation.

weaknesses: The GPS record genuinely places the driver 40 m from the pickup and stationary for 4 min 0 s (F3, F1), and within 200 m of the pickup for 5 min 20 s before cancelling (F2) — so the driver really was there and really did wait, unlike a fabricated no-show; the driver will argue these facts alone show NS-1 (ii)(iii) were met.

The driver never tapped "I'm Here", so the situation is not the classic NS-2 scenario of a driver tapping the button from far away (m_from_pickup_at_tap > 200); the judge may treat this as a technicality and, if so, the fee stands under NS-1 with the default wait threshold satisfiable by F2/F3.

Under NS-1's own wording the record's arrival confirmation is either `driver_tap` or `platform_auto`; F5 says the platform 'recorded driver arrival' at 22:41:30, which the driver may argue is a platform_auto arrival satisfying NS-1(i) even though F6 says otherwise — my case depends on reading F6 as controlling.
The driver has a long, clean record (4.7 years, 4.87 rating, 951 trips, 0 disputes upheld, F17), so a flag_account request against the driver is not supported and would look retaliatory.

claims.assertion: The GPS record shows the driver reached the pick-up area and stayed there: closest approach 34 m (F1), first within 200 m at 22:41:30 (F2), and stationary for 4 min 0 s at 22:42:50–22:46:50 only 40 m from the pick-up point (F3) — so he was physically present, not avoiding the rider.

The driver waited at the pick-up well beyond the threshold: the platform recorded arrival at 22:41:30 and cancellation came 5 min 20 s later (F5), with cumulative time inside 200 m of 5 min 20 s (F2); the $6.61 fee was assessed on that record (F4).

The rider never appeared: the driver messaged at 22:43 "At the pickup point, silver Toyota Altis" (F9) and after four more minutes of waiting had to cancel, telling the rider "Waited 4 min, cancelling" (F10); nothing in the chat shows the rider coming down or asking the driver to wait longer.

Required element (i) of NS-1 — pressing "I'm Here" or an automatic arrival confirmation — is not met: the timeline records no arrival confirmation, driver_pressed_here_at is null (F6), and the driver admits he forgot the button (F12); the arrival that did occur was recorded by the platform (F5), so the outcome turns on this formal step, not on whether the driver was there.

Even if the formal step fails, the equities favour not refunding: the rider's complaint "I was on my way down" is not corroborated by any message in the complete, fully timestamped chat record (F11), while the driver's conduct was transparent throughout (F9, F10); the rider has 0 upheld disputes (F16) and the driver, 951 trips in 90 days with 0 upheld disputes (F17), shows no pattern of fee abuse.

No safety issue arises on this record: the only messages are the two routine pick-up messages (F9, F10) and the driver's written statement (F12), none of which contains any threat, intimidation, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, so SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation is not engaged.

weaknesses: NS-1 (i) is squarely not satisfied: F6 shows no "I'm Here" tap and no platform automatic arrival confirmation, and F12 is the driver's own admission that he forgot to press the button. NS-2 therefore points to a full refund of the $6.61, and on the driver's own statement he cannot claim the arrival-confirmation element.

NS-1 (ii) also depends on the chosen reading: the requirement is that the tap (or platform confirmation) locate the driver within 200 m, and F3 places the driver stationary 40 m from the pick-up only from 22:42:50, i.e. the anchor point of the waiting period is later than F5's recorded arrival at 22:41:30 — the rider's advocate will argue the qualifying wait is only 4 min 0 s and that any pre-anchor movement does not count.

F3 shows the 4 min wait was the total stationary period before cancellation, so if matching noise or movement inside the earlier 1 min 20 s inside the radius is excluded, NS-1 (iii)'s continuous-wait condition is thinner than it first appears, though on any reading it exceeds 3 min.

The rider's account that she was "on her way down" is not contradicted by any system record (F11 merely shows the chat is complete), so the judge is free to accept her explanation for the delay, in which case NS-1 fails and the $6.61 is refunded.

No traffic justification helps the driver: F13 shows only band 3 (20–29 km/h) on Woodlands Avenue 5 and F14 records no incident, so nothing in RD-4 provides a reasonable cause to cancel rather than wait.

points.response: Conceded as to physical presence: F1 (34 m closest approach), F2 (first within 200 m at 22:41:30) and F3 (stationary 40 m away for 4 min 0 s) do show the driver was in the pick-up area — but NS-1 requires all three elements, and presence alone cannot satisfy the arrival-confirmation element that F6 shows is missing.

The wait length is not in dispute (F2, F5), but NS-1 makes each element cumulative: a 5 min 20 s wait cannot cure the failure of (i), so the fee falls away under NS-2 regardless of how long the driver stood there.

The driver's 22:43 and 22:46 messages (F9, F10) prove only that he sent two messages, not that the rider failed to show; F11 confirms the chat is complete and timestamped yet contains no system record of the rider's whereabouts, and no fact places the rider at or away from the pick-up point, so this claim is inference from a statement rather than from a system record.

The driver's own brief and statement (F12) and the timeline (F6) admit element (i) was never satisfied — no "I'm Here" tap and no platform automatic arrival — and NS-1 is written as a conjunction, so under NS-2 the $6.61 is refunded in full; the opponent's own weakness paragraph concedes exactly this.

The equities do not override a failed statutory-condition element: NS-2 is automatic once (i)–(iii) are not all met, and F16 (rider, 0 upheld disputes) and F17 (driver, 0 upheld disputes) are profile facts that cannot decide the fee either way; the rider's uncorroborated "on my way down" is not needed for her win, so its absence is harmless.
Agreed and not contested: there is no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving content in F9, F10 or F12, so no SAFE escalation applies and the case stays an ordinary NS-1/NS-2 fee dispute.
